reference.source: ESC/EAS dyslipidaemia guidelines; NICE guidance on familial hypercholesterolaemia
clinicalPearls: An inherited disorder of markedly elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol from birth, leading to premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
Most commonly caused by loss-of-function variants in the LDL-receptor gene (LDLR), with defective apolipoprotein B (APOB) and gain-of-function PCSK9 variants as further causes
Heterozygous FH is common and often underdiagnosed; the rare homozygous form causes very severe hypercholesterolaemia and childhood-onset vascular disease
Physical signs include tendon xanthomata (classically of the Achilles and finger extensor tendons), xanthelasma and corneal arcus, though these may be absent
Diagnostic tools such as the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network and Simon Broome criteria combine LDL level, clinical signs, personal and family history and genetic testing
High-intensity statins are first line, with ezetimibe and PCSK9 inhibitors added to reach LDL targets; homozygous disease may require lipoprotein apheresis and specialist therapies
Cascade testing of relatives is highly effective at identifying affected but asymptomatic family members
Early, sustained LDL lowering markedly reduces lifetime cardiovascular risk
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hypercholesterolaemia results from variants that impair clearance of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) from the circulation. Loss-of-function LDL-receptor variants reduce hepatic uptake of LDL particles; defective apolipoprotein B impairs binding of LDL to its receptor; and gain-of-function PCSK9 variants increase degradation of LDL receptors. The common consequence is lifelong elevation of circulating LDL cholesterol, which is deposited in arterial walls to accelerate atherosclerosis and in tendons and skin to form xanthomata. The cumulative cholesterol burden from birth explains the markedly premature coronary and other atherosclerotic disease.
additionalDifferentials: Cholestatic liver disease with lipid elevation
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid profile with quantification of LDL cholesterol
Assessment against Dutch Lipid Clinic Network or Simon Broome diagnostic criteria
Genetic testing for LDLR, APOB and PCSK9 variants
Exclusion of secondary causes (thyroid function, renal and liver profiles, glucose)
Cardiovascular risk assessment and imaging for subclinical atherosclerosis where indicated
redFlags: Very high LDL cholesterol, especially with tendon xanthomata
Premature coronary or other atherosclerotic disease in the patient or close relatives
Childhood presentation or features suggesting homozygous disease
Personal or family history of premature sudden cardiac death
reference.prognosis: Untreated FH substantially shortens life expectancy through premature cardiovascular disease, but early diagnosis and sustained aggressive lipid lowering can bring cardiovascular risk close to that of the general population.
pitfalls: Attributing very high LDL solely to lifestyle and missing the inherited diagnosis
Relying on the presence of xanthomata, which are often absent in younger patients
Failing to arrange cascade testing of relatives
Under-treating and not escalating therapy to reach LDL targets
Overlooking severe homozygous disease presenting in childhood
references: ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias
NICE Clinical Guideline on identification and management of familial hypercholesterolaemia
management: High-intensity statin therapy as first-line to lower LDL cholesterol
Add ezetimibe and, where targets are unmet, a PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid to intensify LDL lowering
For homozygous disease, lipoprotein apheresis with adjunctive agents such as lomitapide or the ANGPTL3 inhibitor evinacumab
Lifestyle measures with a heart-healthy diet, physical activity and smoking cessation alongside wider cardiovascular risk-factor control
Periodic monitoring of lipid levels and adherence, with assessment for subclinical atherosclerosis
Cascade screening of first-degree relatives with genetic counselling given autosomal dominant inheritance
Specialist lipid clinic referral, especially for homozygous or statin-intolerant patients
